hero.title: Refactor moves
intro.0: When code already works, why change it? Because the next person to read it - often you, a month later - still has to understand it. Reshaping code without changing what it does is called refactoring. Here you make one small improvement to each of five programs. The output never changes - only the shape does.
task.1.title: Move the behaviour onto the data
task.1.context:
When any code can change a value directly, no one owns the rules about it - a bad value can creep in from anywhere.

**Encapsulation** keeps data and its rules in one class: private fields, methods that guard them. One place to trust, one place to fix.

Here: a loose method in `Program` reaches into `Cage`'s public fields to decide if it is full.
task.1.goal.0: Give `Cage` a constructor `Cage(int animals, int capacity)` and make its fields private.
task.1.goal.1: Move the rule onto `Cage` as an instance method `IsFull()` returning `animals >= capacity`.
task.1.goal.2: Have `Main` build `new Cage(3, 3)` and call `cage.IsFull()`. The output stays `FULL`.
task.2.title: Depend on the shape, not the thing
task.2.context:
When a class works directly with one exact type, it is stuck with that choice - swapping or testing it means editing the class.

**Program to an interface** makes a class depend on what something does, not which class it is. Anything that fits the interface drops in - including a test fake.

Here: `Vet` only accepts a `Dog`, so it cannot treat a cat - or a fake patient in a test.
task.2.goal.2: Change `Vet` to hold an `IPet`, not a `Dog`. The output stays `HEALTHY`.
task.3.title: Hand it in, don't build it in
task.3.context:
A class that builds its own tools is stuck with them - you cannot hand it a different one for a test or another case.

**Inject the dependency** means passing in what a class needs instead of letting it build its own. The caller chooses what to give it.

Here: the `Coop` builds its own clock, so it always opens at the real hour - a test cannot pretend it is night.
task.3.goal.0: Change `Coop` to take an `IClock` in its constructor and store it, instead of newing `SunClock` inside.
task.3.goal.1: Update `Main` to hand the clock in: `new Coop(new SunClock())`. The output stays `open`.
task.4.title: Let each object answer for itself
task.4.context:
One method that branches on a type has to know every case, and you edit it each time a new one appears.

**Polymorphism** lets each type carry its own version of a method. You call it and the right one runs - no branching.

Here: `Zoo` checks each animal's kind with `if`/`else`, so every new animal means editing `Zoo`.
task.4.goal.0: Declare `interface IAnimal { string Speak(); }`, and write a `Cat` (`"Meow"`) and `Dog` (`"Woof"`) that implement it.
task.4.goal.1: Refactor `Zoo` to hold a `List<IAnimal>`: an `Add(IAnimal animal)` and a `SpeakAll()` that loops and prints each `Speak()` - no `kind` checks.
task.4.goal.2: `Main` adds a `Cat` and a `Dog` to the `Zoo`, then calls `SpeakAll()`. Output stays `Meow` then `Woof`.
task.5.title: One class, one job
task.5.context:
When one class does two jobs, they tangle - a change to one can break the other, and you cannot test them apart.

**Single responsibility** means one job per class, so it has one reason to change.

Here: `PetShow` both scores the tricks and announces the result, so pull each into its own class and hand them to `PetShow`.

Keep `Judge` and `Announcer` as plain classes - an interface earns its place when you need to swap a part out, and here you do not yet.
task.5.goal.0: Write a `Judge` whose `Score(int tricks, int faults)` returns `tricks > faults`.
task.5.goal.1: Write an `Announcer` whose `Announce(bool won)` returns `"GOOD DOG"` or `"BAD DOG"`.
task.5.goal.2: Give `PetShow` a constructor that receives a `Judge` and an `Announcer`, and have `Run` delegate to them. `Main` builds both and hands them in - the output stays `GOOD DOG`.
task.6.title: Refactor moves - recap
task.6.context: Every drill kept the output the same and changed only the shape. That is what refactoring is.
task.6.summaryIntro: You added no features - you reshaped code that already worked. Each move has a name, and each one turns up again in the next part as one of the SOLID principles.
task.6.summaryItems.0.title: Put behaviour with its data -
task.6.summaryItems.0.text: a class that owns its state owns the rules about it.
task.6.summaryItems.1.title: Program to an interface -
task.6.summaryItems.1.text: depend on what a thing can do, not on which thing it is.
task.6.summaryItems.2.title: Inject the dependency -
task.6.summaryItems.2.text: receive collaborators instead of newing them inside.
task.6.summaryItems.3.title: Replace a branch with polymorphism -
task.6.summaryItems.3.text: let each object answer for itself, so a new case is a new class.
task.6.summaryItems.4.title: Split a fat class -
task.6.summaryItems.4.text: one job per class means one reason to change.
task.6.summaryClose: That is the toolkit. Next, the SOLID principles name these moves and help you judge when each one is worth making.
